metadata.scope: e_russia (all 270 baronies across k_bjarmaland, k_novgorod, k_opolye, k_ruthenia, k_white_rus)
metadata.hierarchy_note: hierarchy reflects data/ck3_title_tree.json (save-derived de jure tree including x_script_* dynamic titles); downstream localisation/historicity mods should key on barony_key and join against their target landed_titles tree.

schema_notes.vanilla_ck3_name: Exact English localisation string from CK3 titles_l_english.yml.
schema_notes.modern_name: Clean modern/standard English display name of the audited settlement or holding (stripped of key prefixes and parenthetical notes).
schema_notes.modern_name_note: Optional administrative parent, alternate designation, or native-script qualifier extracted from modern_name; null if none.
schema_notes.hierarchy: De jure title hierarchy from data/ck3_title_tree.json (empire, kingdom, duchy, county, holding_type).
schema_notes.anachronism_type: Mutually exclusive historicity category: attested_pre_867 | fictional_placeholder | post_867_eponym | renamed_post_867 | modern_anachronism | early_modern_foundation | high_late_medieval_attestation | unattested_indigenous_or_minor.
schema_notes.is_historical_at: Bookmark-keyed booleans {'867', '1066', '1178'}: true iff first_mention_year is known and <= that bookmark year.
schema_notes.first_mention_year: Integer year of earliest documented attestation for the audited name (negative values = BCE; null if unattested).
schema_notes.first_mention_attestation: Summary of earliest documented textual or epigraphic attestation (or unattested status).
schema_notes.eponym: Structured eponym object {year, post_867, type, details} when named after a person, saint, ruler, deity, or dynasty/tribe; null otherwise.
schema_notes.natural_proper_name: Object indicating whether the title derives from a hydronym, oronym, choronym, or topographic_feature.
schema_notes.morphemes: List of constituent roots/morphemes with form, language, language_code (ISO 639-3 / ISO 639-5), and translation.
schema_notes.etymology_analysis: Linguistic and historical etymology of the audited barony name.
schema_notes.historical_names: List of distinct pre-867 attested names for the same site or immediate predecessor: [{name, native_script, language, attested_from, attested_to, source, relationship, notes}].
schema_notes.source_url: Primary reference URL (Wikipedia or regional historical encyclopedia), or null if unavailable.

b_kholmogory.first_mention_attestation: Local tradition dates founding to 1137 (Novgorod charter of Prince Svyatoslav Olgovich); earliest unambiguous chronicle mention as Kolmogory in the Sophia First Chronicle under 1417.
b_kholmogory.etymology_analysis: Old Russian Kolmogory derives from Finnic *kalma-kari ('grave/burial cliff'), later folk-etymologized into Russian kholm ('hill') + gory ('mountains').

b_arkhangelsk.first_mention_attestation: Archangel Michael Monastery at Cape Pur-Navolok first mentioned in chronicles under 1419; town founded 1584 as Novokholmogory and renamed Arkhangelsky gorod in 1613.

eponym.details: Named after the Archangel Michael (biblical figure, pre-867) via the 14th/15th-century Archangel Michael Monastery.

b_arkhangelsk.etymology_analysis: Named after the Archangel Michael Monastery at Cape Pur-Navolok; originally Novokholmogory (1584), then Arkhangelsky gorod (1613).

b_brin_navolok.first_mention_attestation: Chapel of St. George built in 1722; settlement documented in 18th–19th century parish records.

morphemes.translation: gentle bank (or shortened from surname Brilin)

b_brin_navolok.etymology_analysis: Compound topographic name combining Northern Russian navolok ('low riverbank/headland') with dialectal brin ('gentle bank') or a shortened surname.

b_pertominsk.etymology_analysis: Settlement name formed from the local Pomor/Finnic toponym Pertoma with the Russian settlement suffix -insk.

b_lopshenga.etymology_analysis: Substrate Northern Russian/Finnic hydronymic formation in -enga.

b_onega.first_mention_attestation: Ust-Onega pogost mentioned in the 1137 Statute of Prince Svyatoslav Olgovich of Novgorod; town chartered in 1780.
b_onega.etymology_analysis: Named directly after the Onega River, derived from Finnic/Saami *eno-joki ('great river, main current').

b_pole.first_mention_attestation: Rural village in Onezhsky District; Epiphany Church built 1853–1855, with no pre-867 attestation.
b_pole.etymology_analysis: From Russian pole ('field, open clearing') or Karelian puoli / Veps pol ('side, edge').

b_korelskoye.first_mention_attestation: Documented as a village in Turchasovsky stan of Kargopolsky uyezd by 1888; no medieval attestation.
b_korelskoye.etymology_analysis: Russian ethnonymic village name derived from Korela (Karelians) + -skoye.

b_malashuyka.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1638 as a possession (votchina) of Kozheozersky Monastery.
b_malashuyka.etymology_analysis: Named after the Maloshuyka River, a Slavic-Finnic hybrid combining Russian malo- ('small') with Finnic substrate -shuyka.

b_povenets.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1496 in the Cadastre of the Obonezhskaya Pyatina (Pistsovaya kniga Obonezhskoy pyatiny).
b_povenets.etymology_analysis: Russian settlement name (Karelian Povenča), likely from po- + venets or adapted from a local Finnic hydronym/toponym.

b_malenga.first_mention_attestation: Railway station Malenga constructed in 1942; settlement named after the Malenga River.
b_malenga.etymology_analysis: Named directly after the Malenga River in Belomorsky District, Karelia (Karelian Malen'gu), bearing the Northern substrate hydronymic suffix -enga.

b_yangary.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical or modern Wikipedia/scholarly sources; appears to be an unverified CK3 sub-barony name in Karelia.
b_yangary.etymology_analysis: Putatively Finnic/Karelian substrate name (cf. jänkä 'peat bog'), but lacks verified historical attestation.

b_kustranda.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical or modern Wikipedia/scholarly sources; appears to be an unverified CK3 sub-barony name in Karelia.
b_kustranda.etymology_analysis: Resembles a Finnic/Karelian compound (kuusi 'spruce' + ranta 'shore'), but lacks verified historical attestation.

b_pudozh.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in written sources in 1382 as Pudoga; also attested in Novgorod birch-bark letter No. 131 (1370s–1390s).
b_pudozh.etymology_analysis: From Veps/Karelian pudas ('river arm, side channel'), adapted into Old Russian as Pudoga / Pudozh.

b_vershinino.first_mention_attestation: Rural village on Lake Kenozero documented in 19th-century Olonets Governorate records; no pre-867 attestation.
b_vershinino.etymology_analysis: Russian settlement name derived from vershina ('headwaters/summit') + -ino.

b_yarnema.first_mention_attestation: Rural village in Plesetsky District, Arkhangelsk Oblast; documented in 20th-century administrative records with no pre-867 attestation.
b_yarnema.etymology_analysis: Finnic substrate toponym meaning 'lake headland' (cf. Karelian/Finnish järvi 'lake' + niemi 'cape/headland').

b_kargopol.first_mention_attestation: Probable founding year 1146; first explicit written mention in the Ustyug Chronicle under 1378.
b_kargopol.etymology_analysis: Semi-calque from Finnic into Russian: *karhu-peldo ('bear field') or *kargo-peldo ('crow field'), with Finnic peldo translated to Russian pole.

b_vitzgora.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical or modern Wikipedia/scholarly sources; unverified CK3 sub-barony in Kargopol.
b_vitzgora.etymology_analysis: Contains Russian gora ('hill/mountain') with an unattested first element Vitz-.

b_ostrov_BJA.first_mention_attestation: Ilyinsky Ostrov in Kargopolsky Uyezd documented in 1873 (with a nearby Neolithic archaeological site, but no pre-867 written name).

b_kirillov.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1397 when Moscow monk St. Kirill of Beloozero established the Kirillo-Belozersky Monastery on Lake Siverskoye; proclaimed town in 1776.

eponym.details: Named after St. Kirill of Beloozero (1337–1427), founder of the Kirillo-Belozersky Monastery in 1397.

b_kirillov.etymology_analysis: Possessive formation from the personal name of St. Kirill of Beloozero.

b_dvinitza.first_mention_attestation: Named after the Dvinitsa River (left tributary of the Sukhona in Vologda Oblast); no pre-867 settlement attestation.

b_pelsina.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical or modern Wikipedia/scholarly sources; unverified CK3 sub-barony in Kirillov (possibly a variant of Pelshma).
b_pelsina.etymology_analysis: Unverified CK3 toponym, possibly a corruption of Pelshma, lacking historical attestation.

b_totma.first_mention_attestation: Founded/first mentioned in 1137 in the Statute of Prince Svyatoslav Olgovich of Novgorod.
b_totma.etymology_analysis: Finno-Ugric (Permic/Komi) toponym from *tod-ma ('damp, marshy spruce land').

b_tasta.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical or modern Wikipedia/scholarly sources; unverified CK3 sub-barony in Totma.
b_tasta.etymology_analysis: Unverified CK3 sub-barony name without historical or linguistic attestation in Totma.

b_tischna.first_mention_attestation: Likely corresponds to the Tiksna River (tributary of the Sukhona in Totemsky District, Vologda Oblast); no pre-867 attestation.
b_tischna.etymology_analysis: Probable rendering of the Tiksna River hydronym in Totemsky District.

b_kadnikov.first_mention_attestation: Guard post established in 1492 on Kadnikovskaya pustosh to protect the trade route; town status granted in 1780.

eponym.details: Named after a personal nickname Kadnik ('cooper'), attested in the 1492 Kadnikovskaya pustosh.

b_kadnikov.etymology_analysis: Possessive settlement name derived from the Russian personal nickname Kadnik ('cooper').

b_kevrola.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the 1137 Statute of Prince Svyatoslav Olgovich of Novgorod.
b_kevrola.etymology_analysis: Substrate Finnic/Permic toponym (Old Russian Kevrola / Kevrol / Kegrol) with the Finnic locative suffix -la.

b_verkola.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in a cadastre extract (sotnaya zapis) in 1552.
b_verkola.etymology_analysis: Substrate Northern toponym in -ola on the Pinega River.

b_osmova.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical or modern Wikipedia/scholarly sources; unverified CK3 sub-barony in Kevrola.
b_osmova.etymology_analysis: Unverified CK3 sub-barony name without historical attestation.

b_shenkursk.first_mention_attestation: Vaga/Shenkursk pogost mentioned in the 1137 Statute of Prince Svyatoslav Olgovich of Novgorod; Shenkursky pogost attested in 1315.
b_shenkursk.etymology_analysis: Originally Shenga-Kurya ('settlement on the oxbow/bay of the Shenga River'), later Russianized to Shenkurye and Shenkursk.

b_krasny_bor.first_mention_attestation: Modern settlement in Arkhangelsk Oblast; no medieval or pre-867 attestation.
b_krasny_bor.etymology_analysis: Descriptive Russian topographic name meaning 'Red/Beautiful Pine Forest'.

b_bereznik.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1676 (historically Semyonovskoye; renamed Bereznik in 1962).

b_veliky_ustyug.first_mention_attestation: Novgorod pogosts in the region attested in the 1137 Statute of Prince Svyatoslav Olgovich; predecessor town Gleden founded 1178, Ustyug early 13th c.
b_veliky_ustyug.etymology_analysis: Originally Ustyug ('mouth of the Yug River'), with the honorific Veliky ('Great') added later.

b_nyuksenitsa.etymology_analysis: Named directly after the Nyuksenitsa River.

b_kotlas.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Kodlas in a 1617–1625 document; chartered as a town in 1917.
b_kotlas.etymology_analysis: Named after the Kotlas River; -las reflects Finnic *laksi / Veps laks ('bay, inlet').

b_usyorga.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical or modern Wikipedia/scholarly sources; unverified CK3 sub-barony in Ustyug.
b_usyorga.etymology_analysis: Unverified CK3 sub-barony name without historical attestation.

b_velsk.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1137 in the Statute of Prince Svyatoslav Olgovich of Novgorod; 1397 chronicle as volost Vel.
b_velsk.etymology_analysis: Settlement name formed from the Vel River (tributary of the Vaga) with the Russian town suffix -sk.

b_verkhovazhye.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in historical documents as a pogost in 1552; posad from 1678.
b_verkhovazhye.etymology_analysis: Russian geographical compound meaning 'Upper Vaga' (upper reaches of the Vaga River).

b_ous_vaga.first_mention_attestation: Ust-Vaga attested on a late-11th-century Novgorod wooden cylinder seal ('Oust'e Vagy') and in the 1137 Statute of Prince Svyatoslav Olgovich.
b_ous_vaga.etymology_analysis: Russian compound Ust-Vaga ('mouth of the Vaga River').

b_yemetsk.etymology_analysis: Settlement name formed from the Yemtsa River with the Russian town suffix -sk.

b_choklema.first_mention_attestation: Chukhloma first mentioned in chronicles under 1381 (Lake Chukhlomskoye / Chudskoye mentioned under 1335).
b_choklema.etymology_analysis: Chukhloma (CK3: Choklema) is linked to the ethnonym Chud/Chukhna used by Russians for Finnic peoples, combined with a Finno-Ugric substrate ending.

b_gorodek.first_mention_attestation: Generic Russian diminutive 'small fortified town'; no specific pre-867 attestation for this sub-barony in Chukhloma.

b_boborossa.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical or modern Wikipedia/scholarly sources; unverified CK3 sub-barony in Chukhloma.
b_boborossa.etymology_analysis: Unverified CK3 sub-barony name without historical attestation.

b_lyubim.first_mention_attestation: Mentioned in the Galich Chronicle under 1535 and in a 1538 charter of Elena Glinskaya (nearby Obnora monastery records date to 1379).
b_lyubim.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old Russian personal name Lyubim or adjective lyubimy ('beloved').

b_razlivnoye.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical or modern Wikipedia/scholarly sources; unverified CK3 sub-barony in Lyubim.
b_razlivnoye.etymology_analysis: Russian adjectival formation from razliv ('flood, overflow').

b_soligalich.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in chronicles in 1335 as Sol Galichskaya.
b_soligalich.etymology_analysis: Compound from Old Russian Sol Galichskaya ('Salt of Galich'), referring to saltworks belonging to Galich.

b_onsthia.first_mention_attestation: Unzha (CK3: Onsthia) first mentioned in chronicles under 1219; founded in the late 12th–early 13th century.
b_onsthia.etymology_analysis: Named after the Unzha River (historically Unezha), of Finno-Ugric (Merya/Mari) substrate origin.

b_karitsa.first_mention_attestation: Settlement of Karitsa in Totemsky District formed in 1965; named after the Karitsa River.
b_karitsa.etymology_analysis: Named directly after the Karitsa River (tributary of the Tolshma).

b_suday.first_mention_attestation: First written mention of Suday dates to 1542.
b_suday.etymology_analysis: Substrate toponym of probable Finno-Ugric (Meryan) origin; folk-etymologized in Russian as 'Sud-ay'.

b_vologda.first_mention_attestation: Official founding and first chronicle mention in 1147.
b_vologda.etymology_analysis: Named directly after the Vologda River, derived from Finno-Ugric/Veps *valgeda ('clear, white water').

b_sheksna.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 15th-century charters as volost Ust-Ugla, later Nikolskoye, and renamed Sheksna in 1954 (Ust-Sheksna at Rybinsk is attested from 1071).
b_sheksna.etymology_analysis: Named directly after the Sheksna River, a pre-Slavic Finno-Ugric hydronym.

b_gryazovets.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned on June 17, 1538 as pochinok Gryazovitsky.
b_gryazovets.etymology_analysis: Russian settlement name derived from gryaz ('mud, bog, mire') + -ovets.

b_danilov.first_mention_attestation: Mentioned as village Danilovskoye in a charter of Grand Prince Vasily II dated March 20, 1457.

eponym.details: Named after Prince Daniil of Moscow (1261–1303) / Danilovskoye estate.

b_danilov.etymology_analysis: Possessive settlement name from the personal name Daniil (Prince Daniil of Moscow).

b_vyatskoye.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in a 1473–1489 charter (referring to events ~60 years earlier in the early 15th century).
b_vyatskoye.etymology_analysis: Russian adjectival settlement name linked to the Vyatichi or Vyatka.

b_bezichi.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1137 as Bezhichi (Бежицы), a Novgorodian settlement on the Mologa River; Bezhetsky Verkh appears in the Novgorod First Chronicle in 1196.
b_bezichi.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old East Slavic *běžь* ('refugees, fugitives') with the collective suffix *-iči*, reflecting tradition that the settlement was founded by fugitives from Novgorod.

b_zhelezny_ustyug.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Uglich Chronicle under 1252 as Ustyug Zhelezny / Zhelezny Ustyug (Устюг-Железный).

morphemes.translation: iron (referring to Zheleznoye Pole bog-iron deposits)
river name element (mouth of the Izhina into the Mologa)

b_zhelezny_ustyug.etymology_analysis: Compound of Russian *zhelezny* ('iron', after the bog-iron ore of Zheleznoye Pole) and *Ustyug* (from *ustye* 'river mouth' of the Izhina River at the Mologa).

b_luki.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Novgorod First Chronicle under 1166 as Luki on the Lovat River (and in mid-12th-century Novgorod birchbark letters).
b_luki.etymology_analysis: Plural of Old East Slavic *luka* ('bend, curve, meander'), describing the sharp meanders of the Lovat River at the site; the epithet *Velikiye* ('Great') was added in 1406.

b_kholm_NOV.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1144 as Kholm (Холмский погост / Холм) in Novgorodian sources (later Kholmsky Posad).
b_kholm_NOV.etymology_analysis: From Old East Slavic *kholmъ* ('hill'), referring to the elevated promontory at the confluence of the Lovat and Kunia rivers (with a secondary scholarly hypothesis linking it to Old Norse *holmr* 'river island/promontory').

b_seltsa_u_nishi.first_mention_attestation: First attested around 1495 in the Novgorod cadastral book (pistsovaya kniga) as 'Seltso u Nishi' (Сельцо у Ниши), near modern Proletary.
b_seltsa_u_nishi.etymology_analysis: Russian descriptive settlement name meaning 'little villages at the Nisha [River]', combining *seltso*/*seltsa* ('hamlet/manor village') with the prepositional river locator *u Nishi*.

b_torzhok.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in Russian chronicles under 1139 as Novy Torg (Новый Торг); archaeological layers date to the turn of the 10th–11th centuries.
b_torzhok.etymology_analysis: Diminutive of Old East Slavic *torgъ* ('market, trading post'), from earlier *Novy Torg* ('New Market').

b_klichen.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1371 in a letter from Grand Duke Algirdas of Lithuania to the Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople as the fortified island settlement of Klichen.
b_klichen.etymology_analysis: Medieval Russian townlet (*gorodok Klichen*) on Klichen Island in Lake Seliger, predecessor to Ostashkov; the name is of disputed Old East Slavic or Finnic substrate origin.

b_valday.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in chronicles/cadastral records in 1495 as a settlement in the Derevskaya Pyatina of the Novgorod land.

morphemes.translation: name of Lake Valdayskoye and the Valdai Hills

b_valday.etymology_analysis: Derived from the pre-Slavic (Finnic or Baltic) hydronym/oronym of Lake Valdayskoye and the surrounding Valdai Hills.

b_vyshny_volochyok.first_mention_attestation: First attested as a settlement in 1437 (in Metropolitan Isidore's journey to the Council of Florence) and in 1471 chronicles; the portage itself is noted in 1196.
b_vyshny_volochyok.etymology_analysis: From Old East Slavic *vyshny* ('upper') and *volochyok* ('small portage' between the Tsna and Tvertsa rivers), distinguishing it from the lower portage on the Msta.

b_novgorod.first_mention_attestation: Retrospectively mentioned under 859 in the Nikon Chronicle (and 862 in the Primary Chronicle / Laurentian Codex); 859 is officially recognized by the Charter of Veliky Novgorod.
b_novgorod.etymology_analysis: From Proto-Slavic/Old East Slavic *Novъgorodъ* ('New Town/Fortress'), contrasting with an older regional center such as Ryurikovo Gorodishche or Staraya Ladoga.

b_ladoga.first_mention_attestation: Dendrochronologically dated to 753 AD at the Earthwork Fortress (Zemlyanoye Gorodishche); first mentioned in the Primary Chronicle under 862.
b_ladoga.etymology_analysis: From Finnic *Alodejoki* ('low-lying river', referring to the Ladozhka tributary of the Volkhov) or *aalto* ('wave'), adapted into Old Norse as *Aldeigja*/*Aldeigjuborg* and Old East Slavic as *Ladoga*.

b_lyuban.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the 1500 cadastral book of the Vodskaya Pyatina as the village of Lyubani (Любани) in the Ilyinsky Tigodsky pogost.
b_lyuban.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Slavic root *lyub-* ('dear, pleasant' or an early Slavic personal name *Lyuban*) with the possessive/toponymic suffix *-an'*, attested as *Lyubani* in 1500.

b_soltsy.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Novgorod Chronicle under 1390 ('stali v Soltse'); nearby fortress Gorodok was founded in 1239.
b_soltsy.etymology_analysis: From Old East Slavic *sol'* ('salt'), referring to the local salt-water springs and salt-evaporation industry.

b_luga.first_mention_attestation: Founded as a town in 1777 by Catherine the Great on the Luga River (preceded by 16th-century *seltso Luskoye* in the Shelon Pyatina cadastral books).
b_luga.etymology_analysis: Named directly after the Luga River, a hydronym of Finno-Ugric origin (linked to *laukas* 'shallow' or 'marshy hollow').

b_pushkin.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the 1501 cadastral book of the Vodskaya Pyatina as Saritsa (Saari); became Tsarskoye Selo in 1710 and was renamed Pushkin in 1937.

eponym.details: Renamed Pushkin in 1937 in honor of Russian poet Alexander Sergeyevich Pushkin (1799–1837), who studied at the Tsarskoye Selo Lyceum.

morphemes.translation: surname of poet Alexander Pushkin (originally from Finnic Saari 'island')

b_pushkin.etymology_analysis: Modern 1937 Soviet commemorative naming after Alexander Pushkin, replacing Tsarskoye Selo (1710), which itself was a Russian folk-etymological adaptation of the Finnic estate name *Saari* ('island').

b_pskov.first_mention_attestation: First written mention in the Primary Chronicle under 903 AD (marriage of Igor of Kiev to Olga of Pskov); archaeological settlement 'Pskov B' dates to the 7th–9th centuries.

morphemes.translation: purling water / river stretch (ples) or sand (pesok), after the Pskova River

b_pskov.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Pskova River (*Pleskov* / *Pl'skov*), either from Old East Slavic *plesъ* ('river reach')/*pesokъ* ('sand') or a Finnic hydronym.

b_izborsk.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Primary Chronicle under 862 AD as the seat of Rurik's brother Truvor (Russian Wikipedia infobox also cites 858; fortified settlement dates to the late 8th century).

morphemes.translation: selection, chosen place (or personal name Izbor)

b_izborsk.etymology_analysis: Old East Slavic *Izboreskъ* / *Izborьskъ*, formed with the town suffix *-ьskъ* from a personal name *Izbor* (or *izbor* 'choice/chosen place').

b_ostrov.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in chronicles under 1341 when the 'ostrovityane' (men of Ostrov) aided Pskov against the Livonian Order.
b_ostrov.etymology_analysis: From Old East Slavic *ostrovъ* ('island'), named after the river island in the Velikaya River where the fortress stood.

b_gdov.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the early 14th century (1322 in Russian Wikipedia) as a Pskov border outpost on the Gdovka River.

morphemes.translation: from the Gdovka (Gda) river name (or Old Russian Vdov)

b_gdov.etymology_analysis: Formed with the Slavic suffix *-ov* from the river name *Gda* (Gdovka) or earlier *Vdov* (Estonian *Oudova*).

b_rusa.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Novgorod First Chronicle under 1167 as Rusa (Руса); archaeological layers and birchbark letters date to the 11th century.

morphemes.translation: from the Rus' ethnonym or the Porusya/Rusa salt stream

b_rusa.etymology_analysis: Scholarly hypotheses derive *Rusa* either from the *Rus'* people who settled along the trade route or from a hydronym/salt-spring term (*ruslo* / Porusya River).

b_dedovichi.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1901 as a railway station on the Dno–Novosokolniki line, named after nearby villages; the earlier Nikolsky pogost on the Shelon is attested in 1501.
b_dedovichi.etymology_analysis: Patronymic plural settlement name from the nearby villages Bolshoye and Maloye Dedovichi, derived from the Russian personal nickname *Ded* ('grandfather/elder').

b_loknya.first_mention_attestation: Settlement expanded in 1901 around the railway station (earlier a village and the nearby Vlitsy pogost attested in 1488).
b_loknya.etymology_analysis: Named after the nearby Loknya River, whose hydronym is attributed to a Finnic or Baltic root meaning 'wet, marshy place'.

b_porkhov.first_mention_attestation: Wooden fortress founded in 1239 by Prince Alexander Nevsky on the Shelon River; first chronicled as Porkhov in 1346.
b_porkhov.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old East Slavic *porkhъ* ('dust' or 'white limestone', abundant along the Shelon River) with the suffix *-ov*.

b_sebezh.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in written sources under 1414 by Polish chronicler Maciej Stryjkowski as a Pskov border fortress sacked by Vytautas.
b_sebezh.etymology_analysis: Named after Lake Sebezh (Sebezhskoye), a pre-Slavic hydronym of Baltic or Finnic origin.

b_nevel.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the 1504 will (Dukhovnaya gramota) of Grand Prince Ivan III of Moscow as the volost of Nevle.
b_nevel.etymology_analysis: Takes its name from Lake Nevel (*Nevl'*), plausibly derived from Baltic-Finnic *nevo* ('marshy, boggy place').

b_novorzhev.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1777 by decree of Catherine the Great on the site of the 18th-century Arsho pogost (replacing the 1396 fortress Rzheva Pustaya).
b_novorzhev.etymology_analysis: Compound of Russian *novy* ('new') and *Rzhev* (from the ruined 1396 Pskov/Novgorod border fortress *Rzheva Pustaya*).

b_nyen.first_mention_attestation: Swedish fortress Nyenschantz was founded in 1611 at the confluence of the Neva and Okhta rivers, with the adjacent town of Nyen chartered in 1632 (preceded by 1300 Landskrona).
b_nyen.etymology_analysis: From Swedish *Nyen* (the Neva River, ultimately from Finnic *neva* 'mire/swamp/open water'), used for the 17th-century Swedish trading town beside Nyenschantz.

b_noteborg.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1323 by Novgorodian Prince Yuri Danilovich as the fortress of Oreshek (Finnish Pähkinälinna, Swedish Nöteborg).
b_noteborg.etymology_analysis: Finnish *Pähkinälinna* ('Nut Fortress', matching Swedish *Nöteborg* and Russian *Oreshek*), named after Orekhovy Island at the source of the Neva River.

b_koporye.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in Novgorod chronicles under 1240 when the Livonian Order built a wooden fortress there (founded 1237).
b_koporye.etymology_analysis: Russian adaptation of the indigenous Finnic (Votic/Ingrian) toponym *Kaprio*.

b_yama.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1384 when Novgorodians built the stone fortress of Yama (Yam / Yamsky Gorodok) on the Luga River.

morphemes.translation: indigenous Finnic settlement/station name (later Kingisepp in 1922)

b_yama.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Izhorian/Votic toponym *Jaama*, adapted into Old East Slavic as *Yam*/*Yama* (later renamed Yamburg in 1703 and Kingisepp in 1922).

b_beloozero.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Primary Chronicle (PVL) under 862 AD as Beloozero, allegedly the seat of Rurik's brother Sineus.
b_beloozero.etymology_analysis: Old East Slavic *Běloozero* ('White Lake'), named directly after Lake Beloye (possibly calquing a Finnic/Vepsian hydronym).

b_cherepovets.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1362 with the founding of the Cherepovets Resurrection Monastery (chartered as a town in 1777).

morphemes.translation: uncertain substrate root (folk-etymologized as 'skull' / Veps hill)

b_cherepovets.etymology_analysis: Pre-Russian Finno-Ugric toponym *Cherepoves'* attested from the 14th–15th centuries, containing *-ves'* (likely from Finnic *vezi* 'water' or the *Ves'* tribe).

b_ves_yogonska.first_mention_attestation: First attested in a 1462–1463 charter of Grand Prince Ivan III to the Simonov Monastery as Ves Yogonskaya (Весь Ёгонская); Russian Wikipedia infobox also cites 1564.
b_ves_yogonska.etymology_analysis: From Old East Slavic *ves'* ('village', also associated with the local Finnic *Ves'* people) and the adjectival river locator *Yogonskaya* (from the Yogna/Yognitsa stream).

b_tikhvin.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Novgorod Third Chronicle under 1383 as Predtechensky / Prechistensky pogost on the Tikhvina River.

morphemes.translation: either Slavic *tikhъ 'quiet' or Finnic *tihkua 'trickle/ooze' (after the Tikhvinka River)

b_tikhvin.etymology_analysis: Named after the Tikhvinka (*Tikhvina*) River, derived either from Slavic *tikhъ* ('quiet') or Finnic *tihkua* ('to trickle/ooze').

b_kirishi.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in written sources in 1693 (also recorded as Kireshi on 18th-century maps).
b_kirishi.etymology_analysis: Named after the Kirisha (earlier Kiresha) River, a tributary of the Volkhov, whose hydronym is of Finno-Ugric origin.

b_borovichi.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in written sources in 1495 as a pogost on the Msta River (granted town status in 1770).
b_borovichi.etymology_analysis: From Old East Slavic *borъ* ('pine forest') with the collective settlement suffix *-ichi*.

b_svolensk.first_mention_attestation: No historical settlement named Svolensk is attested in the Tikhvin/Vepsia region (appears to be a game-generated or corrupted barony name).
b_svolensk.etymology_analysis: Unattested in historical Novgorodian or Vepsian records; structurally resembles East Slavic *-sk* town names (e.g., Smolensk) or the distant Belarusian *Svolna*.

b_pikalyovo.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the 1620 cadastral book of the Obonezhskaya Pyatina as 'pustosh Pikalyova' (пустошь Пикалёва).

eponym.details: Named after a peasant/landholder surnamed Pikalyov, who founded the farmstead (attested as 'pustosh Pikalyova' in 1620).

b_pikalyovo.etymology_analysis: Possessive settlement name from the Russian surname *Pikalyov* with the neuter suffix *-o*.

b_vyangi.first_mention_attestation: The village of Vyangi (on the Volkhov River, later absorbed into modern Volkhov) has no attested 867 AD or medieval chronicle mention; the surrounding Mikhailovsky pogost on the Volkhov rapids is first attested in 1500.

morphemes.translation: local Finnic toponym on the Volkhov River

b_vyangi.etymology_analysis: Pre-Slavic Finnic substrate toponym (*Vyangi*) for a riverside village near the Volkhov rapids (modern Volkhov, founded 1918–1933).

b_podporozhye.first_mention_attestation: The village of Podporozhye on the Svir River is first attested in 1563 (modern town developed from 18th-century settlements below the Svir rapids).
b_podporozhye.etymology_analysis: Russian descriptive locative name meaning 'place below the rapids', referring to its position below the rapids of the Svir River.

b_manturovo.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1617 in a Kostroma cadastre (pistsovaya kniga) as the village of Manturovo on the Unzha River.

eponym.details: Named after a local post-867 Russian/Tatar personal name or founder (Mantur).

b_manturovo.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Russian personal name/nickname Mantur with the possessive suffix -ovo (alternative folk etymologies link it to Finno-Ugric *mantu 'podzol' + *rova 'hill').

b_kostroma.first_mention_attestation: Traditionally founded in 1152 by Prince Yury Dolgorukiy; first reliably chronicled in 1213 during the princely strife of Konstantin and Yury Vsevolodovich.

morphemes.translation: river name (Kostroma River), possibly from *kostr- 'fortified place / reed' or Meryan hydronym

b_kostroma.etymology_analysis: Named directly after the Kostroma River at its confluence with the Volga; the hydronym is variously linked to East Slavic *kostra ('awn/flax chaff' or 'fortress') or a Finno-Ugric (Meryan) substrate.

b_galich_mersky.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in chronicles in 1234 as Grad Mersky ('town of the Merya'); later known as Galich Mersky.

morphemes.translation: transferred from Halych in Galicia (likely from *gal- 'salt/jackdaw')

b_galich_mersky.etymology_analysis: Named after the southern Rus' city of Halych (Galich), with the ethnic qualifier Mersky ('of the Merya') distinguishing it on Lake Galichskoye.

b_chukhloma.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in Russian chronicles in 1381 (as Chukhloma on Lake Chukhloma).
b_chukhloma.etymology_analysis: Derived from a substrate Finno-Ugric (Meryan) toponym related to Proto-Uralic *ćukkɜ ('hill, peak'), referring to the elevated lakeshore landscape.

b_nizhny_novgorod.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1221 by Grand Prince Yury II Vsevolodovich of Vladimir as Nizhny Novgorod at the Volga-Oka confluence, on the site associated in Erzya tradition with Obran Osh.

eponym.details: Obran Osh ('Obran's town') is named after the legendary Erzyan leader/founder Obran (Inäzor Obram) associated with 12th–13th century Mordvin traditions.

b_nizhny_novgorod.etymology_analysis: Obran Osh is the Erzyan name ('Obran's town') for the settlement/fortress at the Volga-Oka confluence before Yury II founded Nizhny Novgorod ('Lower New Town') in 1221; excavations found no pre-1221 structures.

b_gorodets.first_mention_attestation: Traditionally founded in 1152 by Prince Yury Dolgorukiy as a Volga fortress (Gorodets Radilov); earliest chronicle mentions date to 1171–1172.
b_gorodets.etymology_analysis: From Old East Slavic *gorodets ('small fortified town/fort'), referring to the 12th-century Suzdalian border fortress on the Volga.

b_kineshma.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1429 as a posad (settlement) ravaged during Tatar raids.
b_kineshma.etymology_analysis: Named after the Kineshma (Kineshemka) River; derived from a Finno-Ugric (Meryan) substrate hydronym.

b_makariev.first_mention_attestation: Originates from the monastic cell established by St. Macarius (Makary) of Zheltovodsky in 1435–1439 on the Volga (around which the Makaryev Monastery and settlement grew).

eponym.details: Named after St. Macarius (Makary Zheltovodsky, 1349–1444), founder of the monastery in 1435.

b_makariev.etymology_analysis: Possessive formation from the monastic founder St. Macarius (Makary), who settled on the Volga in 1435.

b_plyos.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1141 in the Novgorod First Chronicle (destroyed by Mongols in 1238; refortified in 1410 by Vasily I).

morphemes.translation: wide, deep, calm stretch (reach) of a river

b_plyos.etymology_analysis: From Old East Slavic *plěsŭ ('deep, calm reach of a river'), describing the broad stretch of the Volga at this site.

b_shuya.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in chronicles in 1393 (with Princes of Shuya mentioned from 1403).

morphemes.translation: marsh, bog, swamp (cf. Finnish suo) or 'left' (Russian shuya)

b_shuya.etymology_analysis: Generally derived from a Finno-Ugric substrate term *suo/*šuo ('bog, marsh'), or alternatively Old Russian *shuya ('left', referring to the river bank).

b_sol_vilikaya.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1214 as the village of Sol Vilikaya ('Great Salt') during the conflict between Rostov and Vladimir over local salt springs (later Bolshie Soli, now Nekrasovskoye).
b_sol_vilikaya.etymology_analysis: Old East Slavic toponym meaning 'Great Salt', referring to the medieval salt springs and saltworks at the site.

b_moskva.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Hypatian Chronicle under the year 1147, when Yury Dolgorukiy invited Svyatoslav Olgovich to 'Moskov'.
b_moskva.etymology_analysis: Named directly after the Moskva River; most linguists derive it from Proto-Balto-Slavic *mŭzg-/*muzg- ('wet, marshy') or a Baltic/Finnic hydronymic root.

b_kolomna.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Laurentian Chronicle under the year 1177 (archaeologically founded c. 1140–1160).

morphemes.language: Old East Slavic / Finno-Ugric / Baltic debate
morphemes.translation: river bend (*kolo 'wheel/turn') or Kolomenka River hydronym

b_kolomna.etymology_analysis: Named after the Kolomenka River or Old Russian *okolomna ('at the bend of the river'), referring to the sharp bend of the Moskva River near its confluence with the Oka.

b_dmitrov.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1154 by Prince Yury Dolgorukiy on the Yakhroma River at the birth of his son Vsevolod (baptized Demetrius/Dmitry).

eponym.details: Named after St. Demetrius of Thessaloniki, the baptismal patron saint of Yury Dolgorukiy's son Vsevolod the Big Nest (born 1154).

b_dmitrov.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym from the Christian name Dmitry (of Vsevolod Yuryevich, born 1154) with the suffix -ov.

b_naro-fominsk.first_mention_attestation: Predecessor village of Fominskoye first mentioned in 1339 in the spiritual testament of Grand Prince Ivan I Kalita; merged with Malaya Nara and Malkovo in 1925 as Naro-Fominsk.

eponym.details: Fominskoye is derived from a post-867 personal name Foma (Thomas); combined in 1925 with the Nara River.

b_naro-fominsk.etymology_analysis: Compound modern name formed in 1925 from the Nara River (a Baltic hydronym) and the medieval village of Fominskoye (1339).

b_serpukhov.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1339 in the spiritual testament of Grand Prince Ivan I Kalita (sometimes cited as 1336).

morphemes.translation: sickle-shaped bend (serp 'sickle', via the Serpeyka River) or personal name *Serpokh

b_serpukhov.etymology_analysis: Variously derived from the Serpeyka River (which winds like a sickle, *serp*, around the hillfort) or a hypothetical personal name *Serpokh with suffix -ov.

b_suzdal.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Primary Chronicle under the year 1024 (as Suzhdalĭ) in connection with a pagan uprising.

morphemes.translation: to build, fashion from clay (or via personal name *Suzhda)

b_suzdal.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old East Slavic *sŭzĭdati ('to fashion from clay/build'), either directly ('clay-built') or via a personal name *Suzhda (though Finnic/Meryan substrate theories also exist).

b_yuryev.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1152 by Prince Yury Dolgorukiy as Yuryev-Polsky ('Yury's [town] in the fields').

eponym.details: Named after Prince Yury Dolgorukiy (c. 1099–1157) / his patron saint St. George (Yury).

b_yuryev.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym from Yury Dolgorukiy (1152), with the later qualifier -Polsky ('in the fields/Opolye') to distinguish it from Yuryev (Tartu) in Estonia.

b_pereyaslavl_zalessky.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1152 by Prince Yury Dolgorukiy on Lake Pleshcheyevo (relocating inhabitants from nearby Kleshchin).

morphemes.translation: transferred from southern Pereyaslavl ('took over glory')

b_pereyaslavl_zalessky.etymology_analysis: Named after the southern Rus' city of Pereyaslavl (first attested 907 AD), with the regional qualifier Zalessky ('beyond the forest').

b_ivanovo.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1561 (or reliably in 1608) as the village of Ivanovo (merged with Voznesensky Posad in 1871 as Ivanovo-Voznesensk).

eponym.details: Named after a local post-867 Russian landowner/founder Ivan.

b_ivanovo.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym derived from the Russian personal name Ivan with the suffix -ovo.

b_gavrilovskoye.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in a legal document in 1434 as the settlement of Gavrilovskoye (traditionally attributed to 13th-century foundation by Vsevolod the Big Nest).

eponym.details: Traditionally named after Svyatoslav Vsevolodovich (1196–1252), whose Christian baptismal name was Gavriil.

b_gavrilovskoye.etymology_analysis: Possessive settlement name from the Christian name Gavriil (Gabriel), later known as Gavrilova Sloboda and Gavrilov Posad.

b_tver.first_mention_attestation: Traditional foundation date 1135 (first reliable chronicle mention in 1209 as Tver / Tfer).

morphemes.language: Finno-Ugric substrate or Old East Slavic
morphemes.translation: from Tvertsa River (possibly Finnic *tiihierä/*tver 'dark/rapid') or Slavic *tverd 'fortress'

b_tver.etymology_analysis: Named after the Tvertsa River (at its confluence with the Volga), or from Old East Slavic *tverd ('fortress/stronghold'); etymology remains debated between Finno-Ugric hydronymy and Slavic.

b_volok_lamsky.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Voskresensk Chronicle under the year 1135 as a Novgorodian portage settlement on the Lama River.
b_volok_lamsky.etymology_analysis: Descriptive Old East Slavic toponym meaning 'Portage on the Lama River' (later contracted to Volokolamsk).

b_klin.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in chronicles in 1317 as a fortified town of the Principality of Tver on the Sestra River.

morphemes.translation: wedge, wedge-shaped plot of land or river bend

b_klin.etymology_analysis: From Old East Slavic *klin ('wedge'), referring to the wedge-shaped spit of land formed by a bend in the Sestra River.

b_kashin.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in Russian chronicles under the year 1238 when it was sacked during the Mongol invasion.
b_kashin.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym from the Old Russian personal name/nickname Kasha (or alternatively linked to the Kashinka River).

b_vladimir.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 990 (or founded in 1108 by Vladimir Monomakh according to the Lvov Chronicle and Soviet-era historiography).

eponym.details: Named after either Vladimir the Great (c. 958–1015) or Vladimir II Monomakh (1053–1125), both post-867.

b_vladimir.etymology_analysis: Named after its princely founder (Vladimir the Great in 990 or Vladimir Monomakh in 1108), from the Slavic compound personal name Volodiměr.

b_starodub-on-the-klyazma.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1152 by Prince Yury Dolgorukiy on the Klyazma River.

morphemes.language: English translation of Russian na Klyazme

b_starodub-on-the-klyazma.etymology_analysis: Named by migrants/princes after Starodub ('Old Oak') in Severia, with the river locator 'on the Klyazma'.

b_volochok.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in chronicles in 1471 as Vyshny Volochok ('Upper Little Portage') on the Tsna-Tvertsa portage.
b_volochok.etymology_analysis: Diminutive of Old East Slavic *volok ('portage'), referring to the short overland boat-portage between the Tsna and Tvertsa rivers.

b_sudogda.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in written documents in 1552 as a postal station/sloboda on the Sudogda River (with some local references to 1529).
b_sudogda.etymology_analysis: Named directly after the Sudogda River, a Finno-Ugric substrate hydronym.

b_yegoryevsk.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1462 as the village of Vysokoye; renamed Yegoryevsk and granted town status in 1778.
b_yegoryevsk.etymology_analysis: Renamed Yegoryevsk in 1778 after St. George (Russian folk form Yegory), patron of the local church; originally the 1462 village of Vysokoye ('High Place').

b_yaroslavl.first_mention_attestation: Traditionally founded in 1010 by Prince Yaroslav the Wise; first reliably mentioned in chronicles under 1071.

eponym.details: Named after Prince Yaroslav I the Wise (c. 978–1054), who founded it around 1010.

b_yaroslavl.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym formed from the personal name Yaroslav with the archaic Slavic possessive suffix *-jĭ.

b_rostov.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Primary Chronicle under the year 862 AD as one of the towns subject to Rurik (with Meryan/Viking Sarskoye Gorodishche preceding it nearby).

morphemes.translation: personal name Rost (short form of Rostislav)

b_rostov.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym from the Slavic personal name Rost (cf. Rostislav) with the suffix -ov; attested in the Primary Chronicle in 862 AD.

b_uglich.first_mention_attestation: First reliably documented in the Hypatian Chronicle under 1148 as Ugliche Pole ('Corner Field'); late local chronicles give a legendary 937 AD foundation.
b_uglich.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old East Slavic *ugol ('corner, angle'), referring to the sharp bend in the Volga River at this point (or alternatively charcoal-burning *ugol').

b_mologa.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1149 (at the mouth of the Mologa River; existed as a town from the 12th century until submerged by the Rybinsk Reservoir in the 1940s).
b_mologa.etymology_analysis: Named directly after the Mologa River, a substrate hydronym of Finno-Ugric or Baltic origin.

b_murom.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Primary Chronicle under the year 862 AD as the seat of the Finnic Muroma people.

morphemes.translation: the Muroma people (possibly 'highland/dry-land people', cf. Mari/Finnic *mura/*maa)

b_murom.etymology_analysis: Named after the Muroma, a Finnic tribe inhabiting the lower Oka; attested in the Primary Chronicle in 862 AD.

b_gorodets-meshchyorsky.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1152 by Prince Yury Dolgorukiy as Grodets / Gorodets Meshchyorsky (later Kasimov).
b_gorodets-meshchyorsky.etymology_analysis: Means 'Fortified Town of the Meshchyora', combining Slavic *gorodets with the ethnonym of the local Finnic Meshchyora people.

b_vyksa.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1765 as an ironworks settlement by the Batashev brothers on the Vyksa River.
b_vyksa.etymology_analysis: Named after the Vyksa River; Aleksandr Matveyev derives it from Meryan *weksä ('lake outflow').

b_pavlovo.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in a charter of Ivan IV (the Terrible) dated April 5, 1566 as the village of Pavlovo.

eponym.details: Named after a local post-867 Russian founder/landowner Pavel.

b_pavlovo.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym from the Russian personal name Pavel with the suffix -ovo.

b_ryazan.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in chronicles under 1095/1096 (now the archaeological site of Staraya Ryazan / Old Ryazan, destroyed in 1237).

morphemes.translation: debated: possibly from Erzya ethnonym, or Slavic *rězati ('cut/channel')

b_ryazan.etymology_analysis: Etymology debated: often linked to the Mordvin-Erzya ethnonym or an Old Russian root *rěz- ('cut, river channel/marshy terrain').

b_pereyaslavl_ryazanski.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned under 1095 as Pereyaslavl (Pereyaslavl-Ryazansky); renamed Ryazan in 1778.

morphemes.translation: transferred from southern Pereyaslavl ('took over glory')

b_pereyaslavl_ryazanski.etymology_analysis: Named after southern Pereyaslavl (attested 907 AD), with the regional qualifier Ryazanski ('in the Ryazan land').

b_rostislavl.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1153 (6661 AM) by Prince Rostislav Yaroslavich of Ryazan on the Oka River (Nikon Chronicle).

eponym.details: Named after its founder, Prince Rostislav Yaroslavich of Ryazan (12th century).

b_rostislavl.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym from Prince Rostislav Yaroslavich (1153) with the archaic Slavic possessive suffix *-jĭ.

b_vaskina_polyana.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1629 as the sloboda of Vaskina Polyana (renamed Spassk in 1778, now Spassk-Ryazansky).

eponym.details: Named after a post-867 local founder/settler Vaska (diminutive of Vasily).

b_vaskina_polyana.etymology_analysis: Russian toponym meaning 'Vaska's Glade/Clearing', from the personal name Vaska and *polyana ('clearing').

b_klepiki.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in written documents in 1619 as the village of Klepiki (later Spas-Klepiki).

morphemes.translation: klepik ('small knife' / 'shoemaking/fish-cleaning knife' or personal nickname Klepik)

b_klepiki.etymology_analysis: From the Russian occupational/personal nickname *klepik ('small knife', or maker/user of knives) in the plural settlement form.

b_tula.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Nikon Chronicle under the year 1146.

morphemes.translation: river name (Tula/Tulitsa River; cf. Baltic *tūla 'narrow/hidden' or Finnic *tuli 'fire')

b_tula.etymology_analysis: Named after the Tula (modern Tulitsa) River at its confluence with the Upa; pre-Russian hydronym of likely Baltic origin.

b_yelets.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in chronicles in 1146 (or 1147) as a border fort of the Principality of Ryazan.
b_yelets.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old East Slavic *yel' ('spruce/fir grove') or the Yelets River with the suffix -ets.

b_pronsk.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Nikon Chronicle under 1131 (and in the Laurentian Chronicle under 1186).
b_pronsk.etymology_analysis: Formed from the Pronya River hydronym with the East Slavic town suffix -sk.

b_kursk.first_mention_attestation: Mentioned in the Patericon of the Kyiv Pechersk Lavra (Life of Theodosius of Kyiv) under 1032.
b_kursk.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Kur River hydronym (itself from East Slavic kurya, 'river channel/backwater') with the Slavic toponymic suffix -sk.

b_rylsk.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Hypatian Chronicle under 1152 as one of the Severian towns.

morphemes.translation: Rylo River (from ryt' 'to dig/burrow', or pre-Slavic hydronym)

b_rylsk.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Rylo (Ryla) River hydronym with the Slavic settlement suffix -sk; folk etymology also links it to St. John of Rila.

b_sudzha.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1661 (fortified in 1664) on the site of an older settlement by settlers from the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.
b_sudzha.etymology_analysis: Named directly after the Sudzha River on whose banks the town was built; the hydronym is of pre-Slavic (Iranian or Baltic) or early Slavic origin.

b_oboyan.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1639 as a Russian border fortress on the Belgorod Defense Line.
b_oboyan.etymology_analysis: Named after the Oboyanka River (tributary of the Psyol), derived from Slavic obo- ('around') or a pre-existing local hydronym.

b_novgorod_seversky.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned as Novyi Horod ('New Town') in Vladimir Monomakh's Instruction regarding events of 1078-1079.
b_novgorod_seversky.etymology_analysis: Literally 'New Town of the Severians', named after the East Slavic Severian tribal confederation.

b_borzna.first_mention_attestation: Founded in the 16th century (first documented in the early 17th century, 1633-1634, as a Cossack town).
b_borzna.etymology_analysis: Named directly after the Borzna (Borzenka) River, from East Slavic borzyi ('swift, rapid').

b_glukhov.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Hypatian Chronicle under 1152 as a Severian town.
b_glukhov.etymology_analysis: From East Slavic glukhoi ('remote, dense, overgrown') or anthroponym Glukh + possessive suffix -ov.

b_putyvl.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Hypatian Chronicle under 1146 as a Severian fortress.
b_putyvl.etymology_analysis: Possessive formation from an unattested early East Slavic personal name Putivoi/Putivl (from put' 'way/path' + voi 'warrior'), or related to the Seym trade route.

b_vyr.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Hypatian Chronicle under 1113 as a Rus' frontier town on the Vyr River.

morphemes.translation: whirlpool, deep pool in a river

b_vyr.etymology_analysis: Named directly after the Vyr River (a tributary of the Seym), from East Slavic vyr ('whirlpool, deep river pool').

b_konotop.first_mention_attestation: First settled/documented in 1634 when granted to a Polish nobleman during the Smolensk War.
b_konotop.etymology_analysis: From East Slavic kon' ('horse') + top' ('bog/mire'), meaning 'horse-drowning swamp', also reflected in the nearby Konotopka stream.

b_starodub.first_mention_attestation: Known from the 11th century; first attested in 1080 when plundered by the Cumans (also in Vladimir Monomakh's Instruction, 1096).
b_starodub.etymology_analysis: Compound of Old East Slavic staryi ('old') and dub ('oak'), literally 'Old Oak'.

b_trubetsk.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in East Slavic chronicles as Trubetsk under 1164 and 1183 (local tradition dates foundation to 975).
b_trubetsk.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old East Slavic truba ('pipe/channel/river bend') + settlement suffix -etsk (-chevsk).

b_debryansk.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Hypatian Chronicle under 1146 as Dъbryansk (archaeologically attested from the late 10th century, traditional date 985).
b_debryansk.etymology_analysis: From Old East Slavic dъbr' / debri ('wooded ravine, dense forest') + settlement suffix -yansk.

b_mglin.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in written sources in 1389 (on the site of a 12th-century settlement, possibly chronicle Zaroy, 1154).
b_mglin.etymology_analysis: From East Slavic mgla ('mist/haze') + suffix -in, referring to misty river lowlands.

b_karachev.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Hypatian Chronicle under 1146.

eponym.details: Derived from a Turkic/Slavic personal name or title Karach (cf. Turkic qaracy, 'chieftain/counselor'), though the exact bearer is unrecorded.

b_karachev.etymology_analysis: Possessive adjective from the Turkic-origin personal name/nickname Karach + Slavic suffix -ev (or alternatively from a local hydronym).

b_krom.first_mention_attestation: First chronicled in 1147 (the same year as Moscow).
b_krom.etymology_analysis: From Old East Slavic krom / kroma ('fortified citadel, edge, borderland'), also giving its name to the Kroma River.

b_oryol.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1566 by Tsar Ivan IV as a border fortress (archaeology shows a 12th-century settlement at the Oka-Orlik confluence).

morphemes.translation: eagle (or derived from the Orlik/Orel River)

b_oryol.etymology_analysis: Meaning 'eagle' in Russian, though also associated with the Orlik (Orel) River at whose confluence with the Oka the fortress was built.

b_kozelsk.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in an East Slavic chronicle under 1146 as part of the Principality of Chernigov.
b_kozelsk.etymology_analysis: From East Slavic kozel ('billy goat', or anthroponym Kozel) + settlement suffix -sk.

b_vorotynsk.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned as Vorotinesk in the Hypatian Chronicle under 1155.
b_vorotynsk.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old East Slavic vorota ('gate/pass') or anthroponym Vorotynya + settlement suffix -ynsk.

b_belev.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Hypatian Chronicle under 1147.
b_belev.etymology_analysis: Derived from Russian dialectal belev ('light-gray sandy/podzolic soil') or East Slavic belyi ('white/clear', referring to the Belevka stream) + -ev.

b_sevsk.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned under 1146 in the Hypatian and Voskresensk Chronicles.
b_sevsk.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Sev River hydronym + Slavic settlement suffix -sk.

b_ust-livny.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1586 as the wooden fortress Ust-Livny on the Livenka River (preceded by a 1571 watchpost).
b_ust-livny.etymology_analysis: Compound meaning 'mouth of the Livenka River' (ust'e 'river mouth' + Livny/Livenka).

b_lokot.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the first half of the 17th century as the khutor Lokotskoi Kolodez near Brasovo.

morphemes.translation: elbow, sharp bend (of a stream or ravine)

b_lokot.etymology_analysis: From Russian lokot' ('elbow'), referring to a sharp bend in a local stream or ravine.

b_chornobyl.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Hypatian Chronicle under 1193 as a hunting lodge of Prince Rostislav Rurikovich.
b_chornobyl.etymology_analysis: From Old East Slavic chornobyl' ('mugwort / black-stalked wormwood', Artemisia vulgaris).

b_ivankiv.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1589 on the Trudinivska land (granted to Kyiv burgher Tishko Proskura in 1524).

eponym.details: Named after Ivan Proskura, son of Kyiv burgher Tishko Proskura, who established the settlement in 1589.

b_ivankiv.etymology_analysis: Possessive formation from the personal name Ivanko (diminutive of Ivan) + -iv.

b_radynka.first_mention_attestation: Founded / first mentioned in 1780 in Kyiv Polesia.
b_radynka.etymology_analysis: Named after the Ryadynka stream (a right tributary of the Uzh) or a local Slavic personal name with suffix -ka.

b_kiev.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Primary Chronicle under 862 AD (Askold and Dir ruling in Kyiv; traditional legendary foundation 482 AD; archaeological settlement from 5th-6th c.).
b_kiev.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym from the pre-867 East Slavic personal name Kyi (legendary Polianian founder) + suffix -ev/-iv.

b_vyshgorod.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Primary Chronicle under 946 as Princess Olga's residence (and c. 948 in De Administrando Imperio as Vousegrade).
b_vyshgorod.etymology_analysis: Descriptive compound from Old East Slavic vyshe ('upper/high') + gorod ('fortified town'), referring to its high bluff above the Dnieper.

b_bilhorod.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Primary Chronicle under 980 (fortress built by Vladimir I in 991).
b_bilhorod.etymology_analysis: Descriptive compound from Old East Slavic belyi ('white') + gorod ('fortified town'), literally 'White Town'.

b_yuriev.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1032 by Grand Prince Yaroslav the Wise (first attested as Yuryiv in the Hypatian Codex under 1115).

eponym.details: Named after Yaroslav the Wise (r. 1019-1054), whose Christian baptismal name was Yuri (George).

morphemes.translation: Yuri (baptismal name of Yaroslav the Wise)

b_yuriev.etymology_analysis: Possessive formation from Yuri (Christian name of Yaroslav the Wise) + -ev; later renamed Bila Tserkva ('White Church').

b_kaniv.first_mention_attestation: Founded in the 11th century; first mentioned in the Patericon of the Kyiv Pechersk Lavra (late 11th c., 1078) and in the Hypatian Chronicle under 1144.
b_kaniv.etymology_analysis: Etymology debated: either from Old East Slavic personal name Kan/Kanyuk + -iv, or Turkic loanword (khan/kan).

b_zdvyzhen.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Primary/Hypatian Chronicle as Zdvizhen' (Vzdvizhen') under 1097 and 1150-1151.

morphemes.translation: Zdvizh River (from zdvig 'quagmire/bog') or Vozdvizhenie (Exaltation of the Cross)

b_zdvyzhen.etymology_analysis: Named after the Zdvizh River (meaning 'shifting quagmire/marsh') or Christian feast Vozdvizhenie ('Exaltation').

b_korsun.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1032 by Yaroslav the Wise as a fortress on the Ros River defense line.
b_korsun.etymology_analysis: Transferred toponym named after Korsun (Chersonesos in Crimea), from Greek Chersonesos ('peninsula').

b_malaia_skvirka.first_mention_attestation: Skvyra is first attested in 1390 (charter of Lithuanian prince Volodymyr Olgerdovych); Mala Skvyrka is documented from 1612.
b_malaia_skvirka.etymology_analysis: Literally 'Little Skvirka', distinguishing the smaller settlement at the mouth of the Skvyrka River (from dialectal skvira 'rock cleft') from Skvyra.

b_haisyn.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in written records in 1545.

morphemes.translation: personal name Gaisa or Turkic tribal ethnonym

b_haisyn.etymology_analysis: Commonly derived from a Turkic personal name (Gaisa) or Black Klobuk (Turkic) settlement name + Slavic possessive suffix -yn.

b_ushytsia.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in written documents (Hypatian Chronicle) in 1144 as Ushytsia.
b_ushytsia.etymology_analysis: Named directly after the Ushytsia River (a tributary of the Dniester), from Slavic ukho ('ear/bend') + -ytsia.

b_vinnytsia.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1363 as a fortress built by Lithuanian Koriatovych princes.
b_vinnytsia.etymology_analysis: Derived either from the Vynnychka stream, Old East Slavic vino ('dowry'), or vynnytsia ('winery/distillery').

b_yampil.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned around 1580 (or early 1600s) as a fortified town on the Dniester.

eponym.details: Named after Polish Crown Hetman Jan Zamoyski (1542-1605), originally rendered as Janpol ('Jan's city').

b_yampil.etymology_analysis: Adaptation of Polish Janpol ('Jan's city'), named after Jan Zamoyski, with Greek-derived -pil (< polis).

b_zhytomyr.first_mention_attestation: Traditionally dated to 884 AD (legendary foundation by Drevlian prince Zhytomyr; first reliably chronicled in 1240).

eponym.details: According to legend, founded in 884 by Zhytomyr, a Drevlian Slavic prince/retainer of Askold and Dir.

b_zhytomyr.etymology_analysis: From the Slavic compound personal name Zhytomyr ('grain-peace', zhyto + myr), or 'place of grain and peace'.

b_mezhybozhe.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Hypatian Chronicle under 1146 as Mezhybozhye.

morphemes.translation: the Buh (Southern Bug) and Buzhok rivers

b_mezhybozhe.etymology_analysis: Locative compound meaning 'between the Bug rivers' (at the confluence of the Southern Bug and Buzhok).

b_rastovets.first_mention_attestation: Mentioned in Rus' chronicles (1176 battle between Kyiv princes and Cumans) as a Porosian border fortress.
b_rastovets.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Rostavytsia River hydronym (or personal name Rost) + Slavic settlement suffix -ets.

b_zvyahel.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Galician-Volhynian Chronicle under 1256-1257 as Vzvyagl'.
b_zvyahel.etymology_analysis: From Old East Slavic Vzvyagl' (related to zvyagati 'to ring/bark', or a pre-Slavic hydronym/toponym).

b_kolodiazhen.first_mention_attestation: Mentioned in the Galician-Volhynian Chronicle under 1241 when destroyed by Batu Khan's forces.
b_kolodiazhen.etymology_analysis: From Old East Slavic kolodyaz' ('well, spring') + suffix -en, referring to local springs.

b_chortolisy.first_mention_attestation: First documented as Chortolisy in 1578 (settlement area attested archaeologically in the mid-12th century).
b_chortolisy.etymology_analysis: Compound of chort ('devil') and lisy ('forests'), meaning 'Devil's Woods'.

b_horodnytsia.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in written records in 1685 as a town on the Sluch River.
b_horodnytsia.etymology_analysis: Derived from Slavic horod ('fortified settlement/enclosure') + suffix -nytsia.

b_novosil.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in chronicles under 1155 as Itil / Novosil.
b_novosil.etymology_analysis: Compound of Old East Slavic novyi ('new') + selo ('settlement'), meaning 'New Settlement'.

b_mtensk.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Nikon Chronicle under 1146 as a town of the Principality of Chernigov.
b_mtensk.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Mtsena River (a tributary of the Zusha) + Slavic settlement suffix -sk.

b_hradyzk.first_mention_attestation: First reliably attested as Horodyshche in 1639 (charter to Stanislaw Potocki; monastery c. 1629).
b_hradyzk.etymology_analysis: Renamed Hradyzk in 1789 from earlier Horodyshche ('ancient hillfort site'), from Slavic grad/horod.

b_akhtyr.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1641 as a border outpost by settlers from Right-bank Ukraine.
b_akhtyr.etymology_analysis: Named after the Okhtyrka (Akhtyr) River or the Okhtyr hill; ultimately of Turkic origin (e.g., aq-tura 'white fort' or 'lazy river').

b_myrhorod.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in chronicles in 1575 when Stefan Batory made it a Cossack regiment town (archaeological origins 12th-13th c.).
b_myrhorod.etymology_analysis: Compound of Slavic myr ('peace') and horod ('town'), literally 'Peace-Town'.

b_poltava.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Hypatian Chronicle under 1174 as Ltava (name Poltava attested from 1430).
b_poltava.etymology_analysis: Evolved from po Ltave ('along the Ltava River'), combining Slavic preposition po + local hydronym Ltava.

b_pereyaslavl.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Primary Chronicle under 907 (and in the 911 Rus'-Byzantine treaty as Pereyaslav-Ruskyi).
b_pereyaslavl.etymology_analysis: Either from the personal name Pereyaslav + possessive -jь, or per chronicle legend (992) 'seized glory' (pereyal slavu).

b_boryspil.first_mention_attestation: Locality first mentioned in 1015 as Borysove pole ('Boris's Field') in connection with the murder of Prince Boris (town Boryspil attested 1590).

eponym.details: Named after Prince Boris Vladimirovich (c. 986-1015), son of Vladimir the Great, murdered near the Alta River in 1015.

b_boryspil.etymology_analysis: Derived from Borysove pole ('Boris's Field'), later reshaped by analogy with Greek -pol/-pil ('city').

b_priluk.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1085 in Vladimir Monomakh's Instruction to His Children.
b_priluk.etymology_analysis: Locative compound from Old East Slavic pri ('near') + luka ('river bend/floodplain meadow'), describing its site on a bend of the Udai River.

b_zolotonosha.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in written works around 1576 when part of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.
b_zolotonosha.etymology_analysis: Named directly after the Zolotonosha (Zolotonoshka) River, meaning 'gold-bearing' (zoloto + nosyty).

b_romen.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in written documents (Vladimir Monomakh's Instruction) in 1096 as Romen (local tradition dates foundation to 902).
b_romen.etymology_analysis: Named directly after the Romen River, a hydronym of Baltic origin (compare Lithuanian romus 'calm/quiet').

b_lokhrytsia.first_mention_attestation: Written records show Lokhvytsia existed prior to 1320 (on the Lokhvytsia River).
b_lokhrytsia.etymology_analysis: Named directly after the Lokhvytsia River, from Old Slavic lokhve ('salmon') + hydronymic suffix -ytsia.

b_nedryhailiv.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1639 as a fortified border settlement on the Sula River.
b_nedryhailiv.etymology_analysis: Derived from the nearby Drygailikha/Nedrygailo stream (from ne-drygati 'steady/unshakeable') or a personal name + -iv.

b_sumy.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1652-1655 by Cossack settlers led by Herasym Kondratyev on the Psel River.
b_sumy.etymology_analysis: Named after the Sumka/Suma River at its confluence with the Psel (or per legend, three hunting bags, sumy, found there).

b_voin.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Primary Chronicle under 1055 as a Kievan Rus' frontier town at the mouth of the Sula River.
b_voin.etymology_analysis: From Old East Slavic voin ('warrior'), reflecting its role as a military border fortress on the Dnieper-Sula confluence.

b_lubny.first_mention_attestation: First written record dates to 1107 (battle against the Cumans; reputedly founded in 988 by Vladimir the Great).
b_lubny.etymology_analysis: From Old East Slavic lub ('bast/inner bark'), referring to timber/bast construction or surrounding linden/elm groves.

b_odoyev.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1376 (and in 1380 in the Novgorod Chronicle; fortress Oduyev possibly 1242).

morphemes.translation: river valley/hollow (odoje) or personal name Odoi

b_odoyev.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old East Slavic odoje ('river valley/ravine') or an anthroponym Odoi + possessive suffix -ev.

b_suvorov.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1949 (town status 1954) as a settlement for the Cherepet power plant, named after the nearby village of Suvorovo.

eponym.details: Named after the nearby village Suvorova, itself derived from the 15th-16th century personal name/surname Suvor/Suvorov.

b_suvorov.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Russian anthroponym Suvor/Suvorov (attested 15th-16th c.), applied to the 1949-1954 Soviet industrial town.

b_grodno.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Primary/Hypatian Chronicle under 1127 (as Goroden).
b_grodno.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old East Slavic *goroden* ('fortified town/enclosure', cognate with *gorod*/*grad*), reflecting its origin as a Rus' frontier fortress on the Neman.

b_lida.first_mention_attestation: Passing mentions in chronicles from 1180; wooden fortress/castle built by Gediminas in 1323.
b_lida.etymology_analysis: From Lithuanian *Lyda*, derived from *lydimas* ('slash-and-burn agriculture' or a cleared plot of land); also associated with the Lideya River.

b_novogrudok.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in chronicles in 1044 (founded c. 970–990).
b_novogrudok.etymology_analysis: Compound of Old East Slavic *novъ* ('new') and *gorodok* ('small fort/town'), i.e. 'New Little Fort' on the Baltic-Slavic frontier (Lithuanian *Naugardukas*).

b_slonim.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Hypatian Chronicle in 1252 as Uslonim (and 1255 as Vslonim).
b_slonim.etymology_analysis: Attested as *Uslonim* / *Vslonim* (1252), commonly derived from East Slavic *zaslona* ('screen/barrier/frontier shield') or a Baltic/Slavic topographic root.

b_volkovysk.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Turov annals in 1005 (and Hypatian Chronicle in 1252).
b_volkovysk.etymology_analysis: Named after the Vawkawyya (Volkovyya) River, traditionally linked to *volk* ('wolf') + Slavic/Baltic hydronymic/town suffix *-ysk*.

b_sokolka.first_mention_attestation: Established in the 15th century as a royal village; granted town rights in 1609.
b_sokolka.etymology_analysis: Diminutive formation from Slavic *sokół*/*sokol* ('falcon') or named via the nearby Sokołda River in the Knyszyn Forest.

b_bielastock.first_mention_attestation: Established in 1437 (first settlers in the 14th century); municipal charter in 1692.
b_bielastock.etymology_analysis: Compound of Polish *biały* ('white') and *stok* ('slope' or 'stream'), referring directly to the Biała ('White') River/slope.

b_minsk.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Primary Chronicle in 1067 (as Menesk/Mensk) in connection with the Battle on the Nemiga River.
b_minsk.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Menka (Mena) River, likely of Baltic origin (*Mėna*), with the Old East Slavic town-forming suffix *-sk* (*Mensk*).

b_lahoysk.first_mention_attestation: First chronicled in 1078 in Vladimir Monomakh's Pouchenie (as Logozhsk).
b_lahoysk.etymology_analysis: From medieval *Logozhsk*, derived from East Slavic *log* ('hollow/ravine') or a Baltic substrate root with the Slavic town suffix *-sk*.

b_zaslawye.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 985 by Grand Prince Vladimir the Great as Izyaslavl for Rogneda and their son Izyaslav.

eponym.details: Named after Prince Izyaslav of Polotsk (c. 978–1001), son of Vladimir the Great and Rogneda.

b_zaslawye.etymology_analysis: Originally *Izyaslavl* ('Izyaslav's town'), possessive form of the princely name *Izyaslav*, later contracted to *Zaslavl* / *Zaslawye*.

b_maladzyechna.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1388 in a charter of Duke Dmitry Olgierdovich.
b_maladzyechna.etymology_analysis: Linked to East Slavic *molodoy* ('young') or the lost *Maladzyechna* stream (tributary of the Usha River).

b_barysaw.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Laurentian Codex under 1102 as founded (as Borisov) by Prince Boris (Rogvolod) Vseslavich of Polotsk.

eponym.details: Named after Prince Boris Vseslavich of Polotsk (fl. 1102).

b_barysaw.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym from the princely name *Boris* (*Borisov* -> Belarusian *Barysaw*), meaning 'Boris's town'.

b_orsha.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Primary Chronicle in 1067 as Rsha.
b_orsha.etymology_analysis: Named identically after the Rsha (Orshitsa) River, likely from a Baltic root *rus- ('slowly flowing').

b_drutsk.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1078 (and 1092 in the Primary Chronicle) as Dryutesk.
b_drutsk.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Drut River (*Drut*/*Dryut*) with the Old East Slavic town-forming suffix *-esk*/*-sk* (*Dryutesk* -> *Drutsk*).

b_babruysk.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1387 in a charter of Grand Duke Jogaila/Skirgaila.
b_babruysk.etymology_analysis: Named after the Babruyka River, from East Slavic *bobr* ('beaver'), with the town suffix *-sk*.

b_zhlobin.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned under 1654 as Zhlobin (earlier 1492 mention of Khlepen is disputed in historiography).

morphemes.translation: channel, hollow, or personal nickname Zhloba

b_zhlobin.etymology_analysis: Derived from East Slavic *zhlob* ('ravine/channel' or personal nickname) with possessive suffix *-in*.

b_kalinkavichy.first_mention_attestation: Earliest historical mention of Kalinkavichy dates to 1560.

eponym.details: Patronymic village name from post-867 Christian/personal name Kalenik / Kalina.

b_kalinkavichy.etymology_analysis: Patronymic settlement name from the personal name *Kalenik*/*Kalinka* + Belarusian patronymic plural *-avichy* ('descendants/people of Kalinka').

b_rechytsa.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Novgorod Chronicle in 1213 as a town of the Principality of Chernigov.
b_rechytsa.etymology_analysis: Identical to the Rechytsa stream (tributary of the Dnieper), from Old East Slavic *rechitsa* ('small river/stream').

b_kletsk.first_mention_attestation: Founded in the 11th century by the Dregoviches; first mentioned in chronicles in 1127 (as Kleschesk/Kletsk).

morphemes.translation: storehouse, timber structure, or fish trap

b_kletsk.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old East Slavic *klet'* ('wooden storehouse/chamber') or *klesch* with the town suffix *-sk*.

b_baranovichi.first_mention_attestation: Village of Baranavichy attested from the 17th century (1627); modern town grew from the 1871 railway station.

eponym.details: Patronymic settlement name from a 17th-century founder/family named Baran.

b_baranovichi.etymology_analysis: Patronymic settlement name from the personal name/surname *Baran* + *-ovichi* ('people/descendants of Baran').

b_pinsk.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1097 by Nestor the Chronicler in the Primary Chronicle (as Pinesk).
b_pinsk.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Pina River (at its confluence with the Pripyat) with the Old East Slavic town-forming suffix *-sk* (*Pinesk* -> *Pinsk*).

b_lahishyn.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1552 (or 1495 in local estate records); granted town rights in 1643.
b_lahishyn.etymology_analysis: From East Slavic *log*/*loh* ('lowland/marshy hollow') or a personal name *Lohisha*, reflecting its Polesian marshland setting.

b_luninets.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1449 (and in print sources from 1540).
b_luninets.etymology_analysis: Diminutive formation from *Lunin* (personal name) or *lun'* ('harrier hawk'), with Slavic settlement suffix *-ets*.

b_slutsk.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in writing in 1116 in the Primary Chronicle (as Sluchesk).
b_slutsk.etymology_analysis: Named after the Sluch River (*Sluchesk* -> *Slutsk*), combining the river hydronym with the town suffix *-sk*.

b_zhytkavichy.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in historical documents in 1500.

eponym.details: Patronymic settlement name from personal name Zhitko (post-867 estate/village founder).

b_zhytkavichy.etymology_analysis: Patronymic settlement name from personal name *Zhitko* + *-avichy* ('descendants/people of Zhitko').

b_mikashevichy.first_mention_attestation: Archaeological settlement dated to 1690; 1785 private estate.

eponym.details: Patronymic settlement name from Mikash (popular form of Christian name Mikhail/Mikolai).

b_mikashevichy.etymology_analysis: Patronymic settlement name from *Mikash* (vernacular form of Christian *Mikhail*/*Mikolai*) + *-evichy*.

b_lukoml.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in Rus' chronicles in 1078, when it was burned by Vladimir Monomakh.
b_lukoml.etymology_analysis: Derived from Slavic *luka* ('river/lake bend, curved bay') or Baltic *lank-* with archaic suffix *-oml*, referring to its position on Lake Lukoml.

b_vetrino.etymology_analysis: From East Slavic *veter*/*vetren* ('wind/windy') with possessive/toponymic suffix *-ino*.

b_hlybokaye.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in historical sources in 1414.
b_hlybokaye.etymology_analysis: Belarusian neuter adjective *hlybokaye* ('deep'), referring to the deep lakes (Kahalnae and Vialikaye) around which the settlement grew.

b_polotsk.first_mention_attestation: Mentioned in the Primary Chronicle under 862 (as Polotesk).
b_polotsk.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Polota River (which joins the Western Dvina) with the Old East Slavic town suffix *-sk* (*Polotesk*).

b_drysa.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned as Drissa in a chronicle of 1386.
b_drysa.etymology_analysis: Named identically after the Drysa River (tributary of the Western Dvina/Daugava); later renamed Verkhnyadzvinsk in 1962.

b_myory.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in historical sources in 1514.
b_myory.etymology_analysis: Plural toponym associated with Lake Myory and the Meryanka stream, likely from a Baltic hydronymic root.

b_vitebsk.first_mention_attestation: Traditionally founded in 974 (chronicle attestation 1021, as Vitebsk/Vidbesk).
b_vitebsk.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Vitba River (from *vit-* 'winding' or Baltic root) + Old East Slavic town suffix *-sk*.

b_haradok.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the 13th century (Vitebsk Voivodeship).
b_haradok.etymology_analysis: Diminutive of East Slavic *gorod* ('fortified town'), meaning 'little fort/town'.

b_gnezdovo.first_mention_attestation: Archaeological complex flourished in the 10th century (no pre-867 written attestation; village name Gnyozdovo is modern).
b_gnezdovo.etymology_analysis: From Russian *gnezdo* ('nest') + possessive suffix *-ovo*, referring to a cluster/nest of burial mounds or a personal nickname.

b_velizh.first_mention_attestation: Border fortress of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania in the late 14th century; recaptured by Muscovy in 1536.
b_velizh.etymology_analysis: From East Slavic *veliy* ('great/large') with toponymic suffix *-izh*, or derived from the Velizhka River.

b_dukhovshchina.first_mention_attestation: Developed around the 15th-century Dukhov Monastery; sloboda attested 1675, town status 1777.
b_dukhovshchina.etymology_analysis: Derived from the *Dukhov* (Holy Spirit) Monastery established there in the 15th century, with estate suffix *-shchina*.

b_mozhaysk.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1231 as an appanage of Chernigov.
b_mozhaysk.etymology_analysis: Named after the Mozhayka (Mozhay) River, widely considered of Baltic origin (cf. Lithuanian *mažoji* 'small'), plus Slavic town suffix *-sk*.

b_lotoshino.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in a chronicle in 1478.

eponym.details: Possessive estate name from a post-867 personal nickname Lotosha.

b_lotoshino.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym from the Russian personal nickname *Lotosha* + *-ino*.

b_zubstov.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in a chronicle in 1216.

morphemes.translation: tooth, battlement, or personal name Zubets

b_zubstov.etymology_analysis: From *zubets* ('tooth/crenellation' or personal nickname *Zubets*) + possessive suffix *-ov*.

b_roslavl.first_mention_attestation: Founded as Rostislavl in 1137 (1130s–1140s) by Prince Rostislav Mstislavich of Smolensk.
