eponym.details: Named after Prince Rostislav Mstislavich of Smolensk (founder, c. 1137).

b_roslavl.etymology_analysis: Originally *Rostislavl* ('Rostislav's town'), possessive form of *Rostislav*, later contracted to *Roslavl*.

b_klimavichy.first_mention_attestation: First references in historical documents dated to 1581.

eponym.details: Patronymic settlement name from post-867 Christian name Klim (Kliment).

b_klimavichy.etymology_analysis: Patronymic settlement name from *Klim* (diminutive of Christian *Kliment*) + *-avichy*.

b_cherykaw.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in historical sources in 1460.
b_cherykaw.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym from *Cheryk*/*Chirik* (personal nickname or bird name) + Belarusian *-aw*.

b_smolensk.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 863 in Rus' chronicles (Primary/Ustyug Chronicle).
b_smolensk.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Smolnya River (linked to Slavic *smola* 'pitch/tar' used for caulking boats on the Dnieper portage) + town suffix *-sk*.

b_dorogobyzh.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1150 in Prince Rostislav's charter.

morphemes.translation: dear, road, or personal name Dorogobud

b_dorogobyzh.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym from Slavic personal name *Dorogobud* (or *Dorogobuzh* in Volhynia, after which it may have been named).

b_mstislavl.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Hypatian Chronicle in 1156 (founded c. 1135 by Prince Rostislav in honor of his father Mstislav).

eponym.details: Named after Grand Prince Mstislav I of Kiev (1076–1132) by his son Rostislav.

b_mstislavl.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym *Mstislavl* ('Mstislav's town'), from the princely name *Mstislav* + *-l*.

b_yelnya.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1150 in a charter of Prince Rostislav of Smolensk.
b_yelnya.etymology_analysis: From Old East Slavic *yel'* ('spruce') + suffix *-nya*, denoting a spruce forest settlement.

b_vyazma.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1239 (Life of St. Euphrosyne / chronicles; territory developed in the 12th century).
b_vyazma.etymology_analysis: Named identically after the Vyazma River, derived from Slavic *vyaz'* ('bog/swamp').

b_toropets.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Laurentian Chronicle in 1074.
b_toropets.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Toropa River (linked to *torop-* 'swift/rapid') with the settlement suffix *-ets*.

b_andreapol.first_mention_attestation: Volost first mentioned 23 July 1489 (as Dubna); Andreapol estate/station founded in 1906.

eponym.details: Named after 19th/20th-century landowner Andrey Kushelev (pseudo-Greek -pol 'city of Andrey').

b_andreapol.etymology_analysis: Compound of personal name *Andrey* and pseudo-Greek *-pol* ('city of Andrey'), coined in the late Imperial/1906 era.

b_ozerski.first_mention_attestation: Generic CK3 settlement label ('Ozerski') in the Lake Seliger basin with no specific pre-867 attestation.
b_ozerski.etymology_analysis: Adjectival Russian toponym from *ozero* ('lake') + *-ski*, meaning 'lacustrine / of the lakes'.

b_dubrovytsia.first_mention_attestation: First written mention in 1005 (later center of a 12th-century appanage of Turov-Pinsk).
b_dubrovytsia.etymology_analysis: Derived from Slavic *dubrova* ('oak forest/grove') with the settlement suffix *-ytsia*.

b_stepan.first_mention_attestation: First written mention of Stepan dates back to 1290 (1292).

eponym.details: Named after post-867 Christian personal name Stepan (Stephen).

b_stepan.etymology_analysis: Eponymous settlement named directly after the Christian personal name *Stepan* (Greek *Stephanos*).

b_liubeshiv.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in historical documents in 1484 (as Lubieszów).

eponym.details: Possessive settlement name from post-867 personal name Liubesh.

b_liubeshiv.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym from the personal name *Liubesh* + *-iv* ('Liubesh's estate').

b_korosten.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Primary Chronicle in 945 as Iskorosten, capital of the Drevlians.

morphemes.translation: brushwood, bark, or sun god Khors

b_korosten.etymology_analysis: Medieval *Iskorosten*, variously explained from *kora* ('bark' on wooden walls), *korost* ('brushwood'), or the Slavic deity *Khors*.

b_ovruch.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Primary Chronicle in 977 as Vruchiy.
b_ovruch.etymology_analysis: Attested as *Vruchiy* (977), likely from Old East Slavic *vruchiy* ('bubbling/boiling' spring/stream), with prosthetic *o-* yielding *Ovruch*.

b_mazyr.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Hypatian Chronicle in 1155.
b_mazyr.etymology_analysis: Originates from a Polesian substrate or East Slavic root (*maz-* 'mud/clay' or ethnonymic/personal *Mazyr*).

b_naroulia.first_mention_attestation: 18th-century private estate/settlement in the Gomel/Polesia region (no pre-867 attestation).
b_naroulia.etymology_analysis: Linked to the Narovlyanka River/stream (tributary of the Pripyat) or a local Polesian substrate toponym.

b_lelchytsy.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1569 (Grand Duchy of Lithuania / Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth).

eponym.details: Patronymic settlement name from post-867 personal name Lelko/Lelich.

b_lelchytsy.etymology_analysis: Patronymic settlement name from personal name *Lelich*/*Lelko* + *-tsy*.

b_turov.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Primary Chronicle (Tale of Bygone Years) under 980.

eponym.details: Traditionally named after 10th-century Prince Tur (attested 980), though also linked to *tur* ('aurochs').

b_turov.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym from *Tur* (traditionally the 10th-century prince *Tur*, or Slavic *tur* 'aurochs') + *-ov*.

b_sarny.first_mention_attestation: Known since 1648 (or 1670) as a village; railway junction and city founded 1885.
b_sarny.etymology_analysis: From Ukrainian/Polish *sarny* (plural of *sarna* 'roe deer'), referring to the deer abundant in the surrounding Polesian forests.

b_selo.first_mention_attestation: Generic Slavic settlement term ('Selo') with no specific pre-867 attestation.

b_chernigov.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the 907 Rus'-Byzantine treaty recorded in the Primary Chronicle.
b_chernigov.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym traditionally derived from a local Siverian leader *Cherny*/*Chernig* + *-ov* ('Cherny's town').

b_lyubech.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Primary Chronicle in 882, when it was captured by Oleg of Novgorod.
b_lyubech.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym from Slavic personal name *Lyub* + archaic *-ech*/*-jь* ('Lyub's town').

b_gomel.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Hypatian Chronicle in 1142 as Gomy.
b_gomel.etymology_analysis: Attested as *Gomy*/*Homiy* (1142), most plausibly derived from the Homeyuk stream flowing into the Sozh River.

b_unenezh.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Hypatian Chronicle in 1147 as Unenezh (modern Nizhyn).
b_unenezh.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym from the Old East Slavic personal name *Uneneg* + *-jь* (*Unenezh*), later evolving into *Nizhyn*.

b_surazichi.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the 17th century as the village of Surazhichi (later Surazh).
b_surazichi.etymology_analysis: Patronymic-style settlement name *Surazhichi* (later shortened to *Surazh*), from *Surazh* + *-ichi*.
